> 以道佐人主者，不以兵強天下。其事好還.

Chapter 29 drew the line: 道法自然 is 和, taking the world and shaping it is 合. Once the line is drawn, it has to be applied to the hardest material — force.

Because the 合 impulse, once there is an army behind it, stops being an impulse. An army is the most direct form of 合: it does not ask whether the other agrees, it cancels the other's autonomy and installs your order.

So the chapter is entirely about war, and its center of gravity is not war.

## The distinction the chapter is making

It is not condemning conflict. It is separating two things that look identical on the battlefield:

- 止亂之果 — the outcome that stops disorder.
- 取強之志 — the intention that seeks dominance.

The first restores 和; the second breaks it. One step of difference, and the whole weight of the chapter is there.

## 佐

> 以道佐人主者.

佐 is the left hand helping the right. Not commanding, not directing from above — assisting.

The 佐 relation is itself the argument: the one who assists does not take the world as his project. He helps the one in charge do what is required, and required is defined by the situation, not by ambition.

## 其事好還

> 其事好還.

What is done with force tends to come back.

好 here is not "likes to" as a personality; it is 容易, prone. 還 is return. Force returns — not as moral punishment, but as the same mechanism: what you did to another by cancellation, you have taught as a method, and the method is now available to be used on you.

## 師之所處，荊棘生焉

Where an army has been, thorns grow. After a great army, there must be a bad year.

These lines are usually read as anti-war sentiment. They are more concrete than sentiment: they describe the aftermath in material terms. An army consumes the ground it stands on. Whatever the outcome, the field is gone.

This is the reason 果 is enough. The cost is not the battle; it is the ground.

## 善有果而已，不敢以取強

> 善有果而已，不敢以取強.

The good one has the result, and that is all. He does not dare take strength.

果 is the outcome that was required — no more. 取強 is reaching for more than the situation demanded, because the capacity was there.

The five 勿 that follow define 果 precisely:

果而勿矜 — don't preen; 果而勿伐 — don't claim; 果而勿驕 — don't swell; 果而不得已 — the action was forced, not chosen; 果而勿強 — don't press for more.

Each is a way the result gets converted into a position. The battle was necessary; the prestige extracted from it was not.

## 物壯則老

> 物壯則老，是謂不道；不道早已.

A thing at its peak ages. This is called not-the-way; what is not the way ends early.

壯 is not strength — it is the fullness just before decline, the top of the arc. 老 is what follows automatically.

The line closes the chapter with a law rather than a rule: the peak is not a stable place. Whatever has reached maximum has already begun to spend its remaining margin.

Which is why 取強 is self-defeating even when it succeeds. The victory that pushes past the required result puts the victor at the peak, and the peak ages.

## What this means outside war

The same structure appears wherever force is available: a negotiation, a restructuring, a family decision made by the person with more power.

The test the chapter gives is 不得已 — was this forced, or chosen? The capacity to force something and the necessity of forcing it are two different things, and only the second produces a result that holds.
